subject: Accidental deaths due to forces of nature in India — the official count
transcription: Read off Table 1.0 of the source PDF, once, and COMMITTED. Every row is in that table. The rows were summed and checked against the table's own stated total before being written down.

supersedes.why: The 2023 edition was transcribed first and then the 2024 edition was found to exist at a predictable URL. The site was briefly built on a year-old figure. The lesson is recorded in AD-16: a document source with an annual cadence needs its NEXT edition probed, not just its current one hashed.

source.name: National Crime Records Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs
source.table: Table 1.0 — Number and Share of Accidental Deaths due to Forces of Nature and Other Causes, 2023 & 2024
source.why_this_document: The only annual, national, cause-by-cause official count of deaths from environmental events in India. One table serves three situations on this site: heat, climate event and forest fire. It also carries the previous year in the same table, so the change is the source's own arithmetic and not ours.

kind_note: These are RECORDED deaths — deaths a reporting authority attributed to a named cause and filed. That is a count, not a model. It is also not the same quantity as the number of people heat or a flood killed. See `the_undercount`.

checks.note: Both columns sum to the table's own stated totals. Checked before transcription.

heatwave.note: The largest rise of any cause in the table, and the second largest killer in it. Heat's share of all deaths from forces of nature went from 12.5 per cent to 23.2 per cent in one year.

climate_event.derivation: 361 + 39 + 2825 + 351 + 18 for 2024; 266 + 61 + 2560 + 239 + 2 for 2023. Addition on five published rows of one table, nothing else.
climate_event.note: Lightning alone is 2,825 — the largest single killer in the whole table, more than every other named cause put together. It is almost never the subject of a climate story.

forest_fire.note: Eleven recorded deaths in a country that mapped 34,562 km2 of burnt forest in the same period. Both figures are official. See `the_mismatch`.

the_undercount.headline: 1,832 is what was filed, not what happened.
why: A death enters this table only if a reporting authority attributed it to heat and filed it under that cause. Heat rarely reaches a death certificate: it kills through heart failure, kidney failure and stroke, in people who were already ill.

Peer-reviewed excess-mortality work for India puts heat deaths far above the recorded figure. No specific alternative number is quoted here, because quoting one would need the study attached and none was attached during this build.
So the page publishes the official count, labels it recorded, and states that it is a floor.
the_undercount.what_it_is_not: an estimate of how many people heat killed

the_mismatch.headline: One in five of these deaths has no named cause.
the_mismatch.note: 'Causes other than above' is 1,626 deaths — more than every named cause except lightning and heat. A page that reads a cause-by-cause table without saying so is over-reading it.

forest_fire_vs_burnt_area.burnt_area_source: Forest Survey of India, ISFR 2023, Table 4.19, fire season November 2023 to June 2024
forest_fire_vs_burnt_area.reading: The two numbers are not in conflict; they measure different things, and the gap is the point. A forest fire in India mostly does not kill people directly. It removes what the people nearby live on, and no national table counts that.

caveats: These are recorded deaths, attributed by a reporting authority. They are a floor, never an estimate.
The periods differ between sources: NCRB counts a calendar year, FSI's fire season runs November to June. Any comparison between them is approximate and is labelled as such.
A change between two years may be a change in deaths or a change in how deaths were classified. NCRB publishes no reclassification note, so a 128 per cent rise cannot be split between the two.
'Causes other than above' is 20.6 per cent of the total and is not attributable to anything.
Nothing in this table is per-capita or per-event, so it cannot answer how dangerous an event was — only how many deaths were filed.
